The Sahara Desert has expanded by about 10% in the last 100 years. To cope with the problem, the Great Green Wall of Africa aims to plant trees in a neighboring area called the Sahel. This mission stretches from Senegal to Djibouti in the Sahel, [[1]] a distance of 6,176 kilometers. Its purpose is to create a(n) [[2]] to stop the desert from spreading southward. And the goal is to bring back biodiversity and help people thrive.
In the Sahel region, the World Food Programme (WFP) is working with villagers to improve [[3]] land that hasn’t been used for 40 years. The WFP uses techniques to change the soil and harvest water, turning these areas into suitable [[4]] locations. The project encourages community participation and education, teaching people how to reform the land.
One technique involves digging half-moons, which are 4-meter diameter holes that [[5]] rainwater. These half-moons are placed on equal height lines to capture water and prevent it from flowing away. About 10-15% of the water caught in the half-moons enters the ground and refills the groundwater. Local [[6]] like sorghum and millet, which have been grown in the Sahel for thousands of years, are planted in these half-moons. These plants help [[7]] the land and provide food for the people. Another method involves digging trenches to plant local crops like pigeon pea. Fruit trees are planted in pits between the trenches to protect the soil.
The WFP has helped plant and renew about 300,000 hectares of land. This work is helping to prevent [[8]]. Thus, instead of leaving their homeland in search of a livelihood, young people are now able to work on vegetable production year-round and [[9]] the local economy. By using traditional and modern methods, people in the Sahel are learning how to bring hope and prosperity back to their environment. The project demonstrates exactly how the most damaged areas can be transformed back into lands [[10]] agriculture, creating a dividing line between the Sahara and its neighboring Sahel region.
